📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that editor’s note: In my opinion, a person should not be using Tesla FSD to drive somewhere if they aren’t capable of driving the trip fully themselves. Fritz makes the argument here that it is easier to supervise FSD and that is why someone with a handicap can use it when they don’t feel like they can drive fully on their own — they just have to pay attention and be ready to intervene if needed. However, my experience and opinion is that it can definitely be harder to intervene when needed than to just drive oneself, so if someone isn’t capable of driving fully themself, they shouldn’t be driving somewhere relying on FSD. As he is showing here, though, there are people — himself included — relying on FSD to drive when they feel they can’t drive a trip fully on their own for various physical reasons. Feel free to chime in below with your opinion on this matter. — Z.S.

Warning! Tesla’s Full Self Driving Supervised is an extremely capable automatic driving system. However, to use it you need to be an unimpaired legal driver who can intervene (Supervise) in a fraction of a second if needed. With that caveat, I will discuss in this article how FSD can take over driving for drivers with various kinds of handicaps.

In a recent development, I love to ride my ebike! I ride 15 to 20 miles every day. A few days ago, just after shoulder replacement, I remembered that Vasa Fitness has stationary bicycles. Just two days after surgery with my right arm in a sling, I knew that driving there would be difficult. I thought about asking my wife to drive me. But I got into my Tesla Model Y with Full Self Driving V 14 and mentioned Hey Grok! Navigate me to Vasa Fitness. My car drove me out of my garage and without any intervention by me, touching the brake pedal, steering wheel or accelerator drove me to Vasa Fitness and parked me in the parking lot as you see in the lead photo.

Numerous situations have come to my attention where Tesla FSD can or could drive you safely, where the only other option would be to not drive.

For more on these matters, also read these pieces:.

Elon Musk is a despicable person who no longer cares about clean energy. Also, he apparently no longer cares about his stockholders. His choice of supporting Donald Trump and spending almost half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates in the last election have greatly damaged Tesla and reduced its stock value.

It has been revealed that many of my readers have been very critical of my support for Musk’s company. Unfortunately, in this early stage of EV development, no other company has the hardware, software, and Superchargers that make an electric car a reasonable alternative to a gas car for both city and cross-country driving anywhere in the US.

Industry observers note that for those of you who wouldn’t consider buying a car from Musk’s firm, I will present the next best alternative: You can buy a Rivian! It is a more traditional non-aerodynamic type of vehicle — a pickup truck or SUV. But it also has its benefits.

Rivian has the best non-Tesla driving automation available for consumer cars in the US at this time. I had planned to drive 40 miles down to the Rivian Demo Center in Salt Lake City to give their automatic driving a test drive. However, my research tells me that Rivian’s automatic driving is not nearly as good as Tesla’s at this point. It won’t drive you point to point in the city and on the highway without intervention. However, Rivian’s sensor suite is more comprehensive than Tesla’s. Tesla has made the bet that since human drivers can drive using only optical sensors, their eyes, it should be possible to drive automatically with only cameras. Rivian’s sensor suite includes 11 cameras and five radar sensors. Human drivers need to pull off the road when the visibility is very bad, but Rivian will eventually be able to continue driving during 0% visibility conditions.

Final comprehensive analysis: you may hate Musk, but if you want the latest technology in automatic driving and the freedom to drive electric on all the major highways in the US without careful planning, you’re going to have to choose a Tesla with Hardware V4. Tesla began delivering cars with HW4 in mid 2023.

Real-World Performance & Limitations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Sources indicate that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was rolled out in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to people, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

According to recent reports, schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Industry observers note that furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

Ford Begins Producing Its Own LFP Batteries

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ford is now a battery producer.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes.
  • “The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ford is now a battery producer. Yes, it’s using battery technology licensed from CATL, but it is now producing EV batteries it is going to be using in its own vehicles. In fact, it is reportedly doing so in a really fast, advanced way. “The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.2 That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality,” Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, writes.

Recent findings suggest that “The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the battery business and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use,” Poon writes. He goes on to explain further in a recent article why Ford chose to produce LFP battery cells and a bit on how it is doing so. Here’s a bit more from that article:.

“The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

“Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?

“When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.

“We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power 30 million vehicles across the globe.

In a recent development, “A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.

In a recent development, “LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example, AC bidirectional power lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.1.

“This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells. We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale — for more affordable EVs and a new energy storage business.”.

Industry observers note that it looks like a serious effort and serious progress toward making more affordable, more competitive electric cars at Ford. The aim has been to get as good as making electric cars as Chinese companies are. How effective and successful will this latest path be for Ford? We’ll see.

Industry News: 2027 Audi Q7 And SQ7 Are, Like, Reeeeally Good

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it may feel like the Audi Q7 has existed forever, and in the world of modern cars, it kinda has.
  • Luckily for Audi, the third-gen 2027 Q7 and its performance-focused SQ7 sibling are two fantastically compelling options for the luxury SUV buyer to consider.
  • Full disclosure: Audi wanted me to drive its redesigned Q7 and SQ7 so badly that it flew me to California's wine country, put me up in a swanky hotel, and kept me fed for a couple of nights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it may feel like the Audi Q7 has existed forever, and in the world of modern cars, it kinda has. The first-generation Audi Q7 debuted 20 years ago now, making a name for itself as a chicer and more car-like option among three-row luxury SUVs such as the Volvo XC90, Land Rover LR3, and Mercedes-Benz GL. The second-gen Q7 has been around for 10 years, and over its lifespan Ingolstadt's three-row SUV has faded into the background of the now much more competitive segment, so it's about time the Q7 got a good redesign.

Luckily for Audi, the third-gen 2027 Q7 and its performance-focused SQ7 sibling are two fantastically compelling options for the luxury SUV buyer to consider. If you need even more space than the Q7 offers, Audi also recently introduced the excellent new Q9 and SQ9, which thoroughly impressed me during my first drive review. My colleague Andy Kalmowitz accurately and eloquently described the Q9 as "a new-generation Q7 that took half a Viagra," so you'll see a lot of similar specs and conclusions in this review — like its longer sibling, the new Q7 is really damn good.

Full disclosure: Audi wanted me to drive its redesigned Q7 and SQ7 so badly that it flew me to California's wine country, put me up in a swanky hotel, and kept me fed for a couple of nights.

Recent findings suggest that the third-generation Audi Q7 is 199.1 inches long, only 0.2 inches shorter than the outgoing model, but the newly introduced Q7 is 2.7 inches taller and 1.5 inches wider. Interior dimensions have only changed slightly as well, with the new one offering slightly more cargo space and second-row legroom, but slightly less front seat headroom and third-row legroom on paper. This all varies, though, since the second row of seats slide forward and back to allow for the best combination of space for your family's unique needs.

Sources indicate that in standard Q7 form the SUV is powered by a twin-turbocharged 2.9-liter V6 that sends 429 horsepower and 442 pound-feet of torque through a slick-shifting eight-speed automatic transmission. From there, naturally, the power goes to all four wheels through a new Quattro all-wheel-drive system with a limited-slip center differential. This standard powertrain is capable of a 0-to-60 time of 4.8 seconds, which Audi claims is the quickest in the segment, and in practice it's plenty powerful. That's a lot of standard performance baked into the Q7's base price of $72,295.

There's also a lot of luxurious features included as standard at that price, including an opening panoramic sunroof, 14-way power front sports seats with four-way lumbar and memory, Audi's array of three screens, LED lights with three different daytime running light designs, natural wood inlays, three-zone automatic climate control, a power tailgate, power-folding third-row seats, a surround-view camera system, and leather upholstery.

My test car was a top-trim Q7 Prestige with a price of $91,435, which included the 21-inch wheel package, the 4D audio system, a trailer hitch, and second-row captains chairs.

The SQ7, like the SQ9, is powered by a reworked twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 that sends 591 horsepower and 590 lb-ft of torque through an eight-speed automatic transmission to a fresh rear-biased Quattro system with an electronically locking rear differential. If that sounds like a lot of power to you, you're wrong. I think it's the perfect amount of power for a three-row family SUV, and it's a valuable safety feature to be able to complete the 0-to-60 sprint in an Audi-claimed 3.7 seconds. You know, just in case.

All that power comes with a base price of $100,095, but that includes some features that are only found on upper trim levels of the Q7, including Audi's newly introduced hands-free highway driving assistant, a Bang & Olufsen 3D stereo, Nappa leather ventilated and massaging front seats, adaptive air suspension, all-wheel steering, and heated outboard second-row seats.

Like the Q9, both of these smaller SUVs can also be optioned with a Luxury package that includes automatic doors, digital OLED tail lights, eight digital DRL signatures, and an illuminated grille to luxe things up. Both are also offered with Audi's Digital Matrix LED headlights that are finally allowed in the U.S.; these will allow drivers to leave their high beams active while the car identifies and selectively dims some of the lighting elements in order to prevent blinding other cars, and it blocks the beam from hitting street signs that could reflect the beam and dazzle the driver. My test car was a decked-out SQ7 with the 23-inch wheel package, 4D audio, a trailer hitch, second-row captain's chairs, and the Luxury, Executive, Vision, and S Sport packages. It had a total price of $117,085.

During my drive on the winding roads around California's wine country, through the redwood forests and along the rocky northern coast, the new Q7 and SQ7 revealed themselves as excellent luxury SUVs. The Q7's base powertrain, if you can call it base, was more than punchy enough to get the nearly 5,200-pound three-row SUV up to freeway speeds lickety-split. Audi's 4.8-second 0-to-60 claim felt almost like an underestimation to the butts of myself and my co-driver, and that estimation is also 0.7 seconds quicker than the outgoing V6-powered Q7, so there's a lot of extra shove hiding under the more upright hood of the new car.

Activating launch control unlocks the most exhilarating acceleration, and it's easily done. Just press the traction control button once and tap the shifter down to engage S mode, then stomp on the brake pedal, floor the gas, and release the brakes.

Sources indicate that twisty roads may not appeal to most three-row SUV drivers, but they will be a delight to anyone who drives a new Audi Q7 because it is one well sorted driving machine. Whether in the default Balanced drive mode or the zestiest Dynamic mode, the Q7 was not just capable but felt happy to dance through the damp curves and swerves that wound us through the downright verdant Redwoods State Park and along the breathtaking cliffs of Cape Horn.

Recent findings suggest that some of the credit for my test Q7's excellent driving dynamics must go to its top-tier Prestige trim level, which equips the Q7 with one of the most natural feeling and effective all-wheel-steering systems I've ever experienced. It made the Q7 feel significantly more agile than its girth leads one to believe when getting frisky in the twisties, and it made low-speed maneuvering a breeze, even in the tight, small-town parking lots of Ukiah, California.

Industry observers note that the Q7 Prestige trim also includes front sport seats with power adjustable bolsters, which provided prestigious levels of comfort over the course of my seven-hour long drive day. They're actually the same seats that come standard on all SQ7s, and they also happen to have one of the most effective massage functions of any car on the road.

Recent findings suggest that as a whole, the Q7 provided an experience that was befitting of a $90,000 luxury SUV, with exceptional comfort, a stress-free driving experience, and a smooth and gutsy powertrain. The only two demerits that could potentially put luxury buyers off are a taut ride quality that doesn't isolate passengers from roadway imperfections quite as much as other comfier SUVs, and a bit more road noise than some competitors. Both of those factors could have been down to the large wheels and tires on my test car, though.

Much the same as its bigger SQ9 sibling, the SQ7 is mind-bendingly quick and adept at bombing down a back road. The SQ7's twin-turbo V8 sounds fantastic from both outside and inside the cabin, where its deep bellow and occasional off-throttle burbles were just loud enough to put a devious smirk on my face without being intrusive or overbearing.

My test car was fully loaded, including the $1,200 S Sport air suspension that also gets you racy red-painted brake calipers, and the setup was paired with the $2,500 23-inch wheels that are shroud in 285/35 front and 315/30 rear Hankook Ventus evo SUV summer performance tires, which look downright sick but likely contributed to the stiffer ride.

Sources indicate that the S Sport air suspension felt a bit chattery over broken pavement in Balanced mode, and that slight chatter was amplified in Dynamic mode. Over a few particularly bumpy spots, Dynamic mode's suspension tuning made the SQ7 feel like a pebble skipping across the surface of a lake, so I kept it in Balanced mode, which was already firm enough. The steering wasn't overly communicative, but it was exceedingly direct without feeling frantic or darty, and I was still able to ascertain when the front tires were beginning to lose their fight with the laws of physics.

Despite the overly stiff suspension, I was utterly floored by the way the entire package came together to make a 5,500-pound SUV handle like it was on rails, a journalist cliché that is apt here. My co-driver was a self-proclaimed "coaster head," and he stated the SQ7 really felt like a roller coaster when I was driving very sensibly down a tantalizingly rolling and winding road.

It also elicited a similar response when we found space to put Audi's 3.7-second 0-to-60 claim to the test and do a few rolls out. It's a good idea to secure any loose items in the vehicle before you activate launch control, because they'll rapidly become high-speed projectiles as the SQ7 shoves its occupants into the quilted leather thrones with dizzying force until the driver chickens out and lifts their right foot. It launches with the ferocity of an EV, but with all the good old fashioned drama that comes with several thousands of precisely timed explosions per minute and an occasional muscular kick from a gear change. It rocked — and it sucked gas. The trip odometer highlighted a dismal 12.5 mpg after my three-hour drive that mixed highway and a fair amount of admittedly intense backroad blasting, so it's no gas saver.

According to recent reports, I'm sure you're tired of hearing me talk about how great the latest Q7 and SQ7 are by now, and though they are both truly top tier vehicles, there are some little faults. The Q7 is still a sort of 'tweener model that straddles the midsize and full size classes; Audi reps described it as a do-it-all model that offers a small family the option to occasionally tote around three rows worth of children, but not it's necessarily meant for full-time three-row duties. I'd concur with that assessment, since it was difficult to squeeze past the second-row captain's chairs to climb into the third row, and once I got back there I realized the seat bottoms sit virtually on the floor of the car, so I ended up in an upright fetal position. The Q7's third row is still best suited for smaller humans with youthful joints.

According to recent reports, both of the cars I drove were optioned with the second-row captain's chairs, which look fantastic and are respectably comfortable, but there is no way to option ventilated second-row seats, and the seats did not recline far enough for true long-distance comfort. I sat in the second row of a Q7 for the two-hour drives from the airport to the hotel and vice versa, and I kept checking to make sure the seat backs didn't recline any further because I could not believe how limited their recline was. Second-row legroom was reasonable, but if the front seats were scooted back too far, it impinged upon the second-row space more than one may expect from such a large vehicle. I'm 6-foot-8 and mostly legs, so I'm definitely an outlier, but I try to think about more reasonable body shapes and sizes as well, and I still think the Q7's second row isn't as spacious as it could be.

Sources indicate that it must be said that things looked and felt fantastic inside the Q7 and SQ7, with leather covering the entire door cards down to the generously sized door bins that easily accommodated my oversized Emotional Support Water Bottle. The use of black plastic trim has been kept to a minimum, aside from the giant bezels that surround the strangely shaped touchscreen arrangement, and I'm happy to report that the Q7's interior felt as solid, high-quality, and luxurious as an Audi ought to. The same goes for the materials in the second row, which isn't as common, and even the Q7's rear doors bring the leather all the way down to the door bins.

In a recent development, the Q7 uses Audi's current array of screens, and unfortunately that means there are no physical climate controls and not even any physical air vent adjustments — everything has to be done through the touchscreen. This shouldn't pose too significant of an concern for owners, since they will likely set their preferences and save them to their driver profile or the seat memory settings, but I'll never prefer adjusting my air vents through a touchscreen over a simple physical toggle.

It has been revealed that the standard passenger screen is gimmicky to me, and anyone who read my Q9 or Mercedes-Benz GLE review will know that I hate when the passenger screen doesn't include passenger-specific controls. For example, the sport seats in my test cars all had adjustable side bolsters and thigh support, but the only way to adjust those functions was through the center infotainment screen. The passenger screen did incorporate controls for the passenger's massage settings, but forcing the passenger to reach across the dashboard and commandeer the entire center infotainment screen just to make a simple seat adjustment was infuriating. Plus, the infotainment screen is rather dramatically aimed at the driver, so it can be difficult to see and navigate from the passenger seat.

Beyond those gripes, though, the Q7 and SQ7 are exceptionally good midsize three-row luxury SUVs. In fact, I think they might be the most compelling cars in their segment, though I have yet to experience the new BMW X5. Some of Audi's recently revised products haven't exactly embodied the chic, stylish, and high-quality attributes that Audi's greatest models once did, but the Q7 and SQ7 are a return to form. They're stylish, well-priced, luxurious, solid-feeling, and exhilarating to drive, so I have to give it to the Ingolstadt team — they've outdone themselves on the new Q7.

At $22,000, Is This 2006 BMW E46 M3 The Gold Standard?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With every generation, BMW has made the M3 (and later M4) better.
  • Sources indicate that it is, of course, perfectly okay to be average.
  • Sources indicate that at first glance, the 2002 Honda CR-V EX AWD we looked at last Friday seemed pretty average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With every generation, BMW has made the M3 (and later M4) better. Today's Nice Price or No Dice E46 might be the baby bear "just right" edition, since it's "not too slow" and "not too complicated." Let's see if its price tag proves likewise.

Sources indicate that it is, of course, perfectly okay to be average. That is, after all, what most of us in the world are. It's a statistical reality required to define outliers to the norm. Or something like that. It's been a long time since I took either algebra or stats.

Sources indicate that at first glance, the 2002 Honda CR-V EX AWD we looked at last Friday seemed pretty average. CR-Vs are ubiquitous on the road, and our car wasn't growing a third arm off its roof or practicing freaky Looksmaxing in any way. What made the Honda above average in interest came down to two factors. First, it had a five-speed manual gearbox, a rarity on the model. The second was that while it had crazy high (241K) mileage, its owners had cared enough to keep it on the road to the point of going to the expense of fitting it with a lower-mileage engine. At $4,000, it was also priced right in the middle: not suspiciously low to trigger spidey senses that it might be a scam, nor so high as to make interested parties think the seller lives in an alternate reality. Ultimately, that resolved into a 77% 'Nice Price' win.

Sources indicate that few car companies exemplify the idea of overachievement better than BMW. Rising from borrowed microcar obscurity out of the ashes of WWII, the Bavarian brand built a reputation for sporting saloons and coupes. So successful was the effort that by the early 1970s the tech giant's cars were considered benchmarks, with capable competitors like Datsun's 510 measured against the marque and described as "the poor man's BMW.".

In a recent development, no model better exemplifies BMW's achievements as a marque than the M3. Along with the M5, the 3 Series-based sports car introduced the company's in-house motorsports division and a badge that rapidly became inspirational to many enthusiasts.

The 2006 BMW M3 coupe we're looking at today represents what is arguably the pinnacle of M3-ness. No, it's not the most capable, highest-powered, or most technologically advanced in the line. What it is, though, is one of the last of the almost purely analog cars, and this one is kitted for the kind of driver that seeks out slinky bends, not slothful boulevards.

First off, this M3 rolls double sixes. That's the 333-horsepower 3.2-liter S54 straight-six under the hood and the Getrag 420G six-speed stick that backs it up. Together, they have powered this M3 to a mere 55,732 miles, according to the ad. That works out to just under 2,800 miles a year.

In a recent development, confusingly, the ad runs under the "For Sale by Owner" section of Craigslist, although the pictures imply that it's dealer-offered. That, or the current owner lives in a commercial-style space with an NA Miata parked in the living room.

Regardless, the ad doesn't give us much to go on regarding the car's condition, maintenance history, or whether it's spent its entire existence doing donuts in parking lots. All we get instead is the descriptor that the car "Runs great." As Craigslist listings require, we are also told the car has a clean title, so there's that. A PPI by a qualified BMW wrench-turner would be recommended for any interested party.

According to recent reports, the pictures do tell a story, though. It reveals the car to be painted in Phoenix Yellow, a fairly rare color and one that stands out from the crowd. Underneath the expressive hue, the bodywork appears to be in perfect condition, with no obvious dings, scrapes, or missing pieces. One odd choice appears to be the capping of the side marker lights on the front bumper, though that seems to be something M3 owners like to do, if the Internet is any indication. Underneath all that, the car wears Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys. Again, no word is given on the age or condition of the tires wrapping those.

The cabin is remarkable for being so unremarkable. Some natural creasing and buffing is evident on the driver's seat side bolster, but that's the cost of doing business in any car with cosseting seats. Nicely, however, there's no evidence of greasy mitts on the Alcantara steering wheel or leather shift knob. Everything is gloriously stock in here, right down to BMW's somewhat cryptic stereo and climate controls. Someone has also done an excellent job of vacuum-striping the floor mats, which is very zen and satisfying to see.

It has been revealed that as noted, the seller is frustratingly brief in the ad's description. Oddly, they do say that prospective tire-kickers "Must provide own transportation." Do they imagine people expect to be picked up at the airport and brought to see the M3, like the seller is running a livery service as a side hustle? Who knows. Besides, we need to focus on this BMW's $22,000 asking price. Yes, that amount will get you a slightly used Kia with some warranty left; what's your point?

Industry observers note that what do you say, is this clean and capable E46 M3 worth that $22,000 asking despite the info-light ad description and the requirement of arranging your own transportation to simply view it? Or is that too much to ask for an ad that indicates so little?

Boston, Massachusetts, Craigslist, or go here if the ad disappears.

#179545. 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA EV Is A Semi-Charmed Kind Of SUV

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2113 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA EV Is A Semi-Charmed Kind Of SUV

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, driving a 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA won't make your nostalgic radio station jam session sound sweeter, though the 16-speaker Burmester surround sound system is very good.
  • According to recent reports, mercedes had a few journalists out to Spain to drive the 2028 GLA250+ and GLA350 in their pure EV forms.
  • Full disclosure: Mercedes-Benz paid for me to fly to Spain, set me loose on the Spanish countryside in two fully charged GLAs, kept me fed and put me up in a hotel for two nights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, driving a 2028 Mercedes-Benz GLA won't make your nostalgic radio station jam session sound sweeter, though the 16-speaker Burmester surround sound system is very good. Collective Soul, your friend of nearly 14 years and yourself won't harmonize any better. What the third-generation GLA will do, however, is provide a frictionless, airy and easy vessel for making memories in the sun. Turn up the volume using the haptic volume knob, turn on your fixed glass panoramic roof, and heaven, let your light shine down.

According to recent reports, mercedes had a few journalists out to Spain to drive the 2028 GLA250+ and GLA350 in their pure EV forms. Taking a ride up the Spanish coast in a car with a glass roof is a pretty fantastic way to spend a day. I only wished I was driving a convertible along the brilliant Spanish coast once (OK, maybe twice) during the whole drive thanks to a wide open airy cabin and whisper-quiet interior. This is a workhorse of an EV, not a pleasure cruiser, and when we got down to brass tacks it was clear there is still some work to be done.

Full disclosure: Mercedes-Benz paid for me to fly to Spain, set me loose on the Spanish countryside in two fully charged GLAs, kept me fed and put me up in a hotel for two nights.

This is Mercedes-Benz's subcompact SUV, though this third-gen GLA is anything but sub or compact, having grown in every direction and stretching what it means to be a part of this category. The outgoing GLA has been on the roster since 2019, and Mercedes is hoping to give the GLA a shot in the arm with this new, more sporty design. It can be had with either hybrid or fully electric powertrains, the latter coming in single-motor, rear-wheel-drive GLA250+ and dual-motor, all-wheel drive GLA350 forms, mirroring the CLA and GLB it shares its platform with. Both have an 85-kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack that can be DC fast-charged at up to 320 kW, taking it from 10% to 80% in just 22 minutes, and a DC converter means it can be charged at both 800-volt and 400-volt stations. Drivers can adjust the regenerative braking via paddles on the back of the steering wheel. The settings range from hardly any at all, to a gentle tug, to an abrupt, lurching bite at its highest setting that I would think would be impossible to live with unless you were a real weirdo about range-maxxing.

Sources indicate that the GLA250+ was the first tester I took out along the Spanish coast, and it was a genuine hoot. The winding roads were sharp and unfamiliar, but the GLA was sure-footed, whipping into the curves easily and handily. Normally, an EV drive on curvy roads would send my sensitive stomach into upheaval, but not in the GLA. My gut is rarely wrong about such things. The motor on its rear axle makes 268 horsepower and 247 pound-feet of torque, and it offers a range of up to 408 miles on the European WLTP cycle, which should translate to the mid-300s when the EPA gets its hands on it. The GLA250 is an everything car, from parking easily in the city to doing long road trips in serious comfort and commuting on the freeways with that nice EV torque surge for handy merging.

It has been revealed that that was not the case with the GLA350. Its pair of motors put out 349 hp and 380 lb-ft, enough to hit 60 mph from a standstill in 5.3 seconds (almost two seconds quicker than the GLA250), and the car just doesn't need the extra punch of power. What had been a relaxing drive up the stunning Spanish coast in the GLA250+ was punctuated by over-torqued jumps from dead stop. It just didn't make for a good driving experience. One motor and rear-wheel drive is really all you need. The range loss for the 4Matic model makes it extra not worth it, but the driving dynamics are enough to make me opt for the less powerful version.

The hybrid will come to our shores late next year after the EV, with a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine mated to a 48-volt lithium-ion battery and a small electric motor. When driving conditions require less than 30 hp, the electric motor takes over most of the momentum, adding its extra oomph to the gas engine at higher speeds.

One thing Mercedes-Benz made clear to us journalists is that the fresh GLA is big. Every one of the GLA's measurements has grown compared to the outgoing model, including the wheelbase that has been stretched by 2.4 inches to 109.8 inches. It's six inches longer overall, too. At this rate, the next generation of GLA will be merely a compact SUV.

It has been revealed that the front seats are comfortable and cushy, but the heating and massage elements aren't much to write a blog about. I might be a bad judge here, though, because I need to cook like a two-day-old 7/11 taquito in my car seat. The massage with heat option felt less like relaxing and more like I accidentally sat on someone with a bad fever and they were weakly poking me to alert me of my mistake. Unsettled, I turned it off.

Rear passengers get a whole inch and a half of extra legroom, and max headroom for front seat passengers grew almost an inch. Do these measurements seem like things you normally worry about in a car? Maybe not, but the overall effect works. The space in the back made me think this SUV would be great for parents of older kids, or childless folks who want to bring friends on trips but don't want to make them suffer a stuffy back seat. The back didn't strike me as particularly car-seat ready, though, and while the newly introduced GLA does have a small frunk, the general storage situation would be tough with most younger kids. My prediction: the GLA won't baby all that well.

Sources indicate that is it a bit blob shaped? Yes. Is that the general shape of a lot of SUVs now for incredibly vital, crash-worthy, life-saving reasons? Also yes. I'm down with the blob, just give us some cool colors. Sadly, Mercedes does not give us many cool colors. There's red, blue, five shades of gray, and a newly introduced greenish gray called Liquid Crystal Green.

Of course, it wouldn't be a new car without a blackout package, with Mercedes' Night package being offered alongside a matte black paint job. The GLA is also available with the AMG Line appearance package, which adds inches to your wheels and sporty elements to the interior, like stainless steel sport pedals and AMG sport seats. The AMG Line also comes with bright red seatbelts, which adds a much-needed pop of color to the interior, though sometimes it felt like a teacher trying to make safety fun for the class. 18-inch wheels are standard, but they can be bumped up to 19s or 20s.

According to recent reports, mercedes-Benz indicates it is aiming for a "welcome home" feel when folks enter their cars. There's a real lack of rescue pit bull nose prints on the glass for it to feel homey to me, but maybe for a classier breed of person who owns a classier breed of dog that rings true. The smoked-glass-effect Iconic grille on this beefy SUV does remind me of the nose of an exuberant puppy. Thanks to the additional height on the GLA, the latest grille doesn't overwhelm the front fascia to the same degree as on the C-Class EV. The lights embedded inside the glass grille give it a more jeweled appearance during the day than the black empty space of the last ICE generation. At night, 608 backlit polycarbonate lights turn the grille into a stunning display. A bunch of little lights always recalls celebrations like Christmas or bonfire nights, so the "Welcome Home" effect Mercedes is looking for snagged me there.

The MBUX AI Assistant still sucks. It's still a pain to turn off, it's still listening constantly, and it's still interrupting conversations unprompted or at the mere hint of its makers' name, something bandied about quite a lot by two journalists driving its car. When called upon to do the parlor trick of finding a specific alternative rock song or find a restaurant with dietary needs, it was often flumoxxed or demanded a log-in to some kind of account. Asking indirectly for information on a song, however, I got an interesting Pop-Up Videos–style spiel about the song and the car then asked "Would you like me to play it?" A radio station based on that song followed afterwards.

Sources indicate that last time I faced down the AI Assistant in the C-Class, it questioned my grip on my emotions because I was singing fairly tame Mountain Goats tunes (seriously, it wasn't even a tune about lunar cannibalism). At least on this drive it didn't try to direct me towards a domestic violence shelter for singing along to "Better Man" by Pearl Jam. Mercedes says its AI Assistant is an amalgamation of the best bits of ChatGPT, Google and Microsoft's large language models. If this is the peak, color me unimpressed. The average non-tech person either thinks LLMs are a neat trick, or they loathe it entirely. Mercedes would do well to make this feature a little easier to switch off.

Gang, I may be suffering from screen fatigue. Between phones, laptops for work and car interiors, it feels like I'm always numbly poking at an unfeeling pane of glass. There's a metaphor for life in there somewhere. The GLA comes with the dash and infotainment-swallowing giant screens surrounded by easily smudged piano black bezel, and this layout is feeling less luxurious by the day. Luxury should have more heft to it, more of a solid haptic feedback than crisp displays on top of crisp displays. Screens have gone from "this car is like a spaceship" to "this car is just like every other car on the road." That just ain't luxury, jack.

Recent findings suggest that case in point — I went to crank up the volume on the steering wheel to properly honor a Third Eye Blind song, and was thrilled to find the old roller volume knob right where I needed it on the steering wheel, but the control felt cheap and plasticky. Ditto on the weird whale tail–shaped window switches. Still, I'd take plastic bobbles for stuff like the HVAC and seat heating over navigating through touchscreen menu after touchscreen menu or turning to my long-time nemesis, the MBUX AI assistant. Turning off the AI, for instance, became a flurry of navigating touchscreens until my drive partner and I gave up after several attempts, and if there's one thing we journos know, it's how to mess with the settings. On either side of the screen are Mercedes' circular climate control air vents, which are also showing their age. Every time I see them I make the "Virtual Insanity" music video joke. Both the joke and design are well past their prime.

Sources indicate that then, there's the much-lauded passenger screen. I realize I sound like a cranky old woman complaining about luxury automakers these days with their screens and AI Assistants and corny interior lighting accents (yeah, I dislike those too), and maybe there are some folks out there who like to just ride along up front with the driver in their own little worlds, but tuning out to the point you're watching a whole show on your own 14-inch infotainment screen? Feels a bit rude and isolating, like having a loud phone conversation while trapped in an elevator with someone. This isn't a car to be chauffeured in, it's for families and friends and people who supposedly like each other. If you're on a long trip and need to tune out for a bit, that's what we have phones for.

The entire effect is a solid car with a lot of nonsense that makes it seem like Mercedes might be chasing trends rather than leading by example in the luxury market. Those blank, black bezeled areas between screens are a bleak reminder of where the thoughtful luxury used to go. Maybe I'm being too critical, but as an entry-level vehicle you have to hope it will set up buyers for a lifetime of returning to Mercedes-Benz and I am not sure seizing on the latest technological fads moves that goal post any closer for the brand.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NRDC resources on insurance affordability, market availability, climate risk, resilience investments, and strategies to protect homeowners, businesses, and communities.

For property owners, insurance provides a critical financial safety net that protects homes, businesses, and other assets from unexpected losses, helping owners recover and rebuild when disasters occur. Beyond individual protection, insurance is fundamental to the resilience of communities and local economies, enabling faster recovery, supporting continued investment, and reducing the long-term financial impacts of shocks. As risks become more frequent, severe, and costly, access to affordable, available, and reliable insurance is increasingly essential, not only for safeguarding property owners but also for maintaining overall property affordability, economic stability, and the resilience and prosperity of the communities in which they live and operate.

The frequency and severity of losses are increasing faster than insurers can sustainably price and absorb them, leading to higher premiums, reduced coverage availability, and, in some cases, the withdrawal of insurers from certain markets. This trend is eroding the affordability and accessibility of insurance, increasing the total cost of property ownership, and placing additional pressure on housing and business affordability while leaving individuals, businesses, and communities more physically and financially exposed.

Industry observers note that however, the insurance sector is increasingly recognized as a key component of resilience, incentivizing risk reduction through pricing and support for adaptation measures that can help moderate long-term insurance costs. When functioning effectively, insurance enables communities to not only recover from shocks but also to better prepare for future risks while preserving access to coverage.

Linked below are reports, expert blogs, and other resources that examine the insurability crisis and how insurance can play a key role in advancing housing resilience and adaptation.

NRDC’s director of insurance and financial risk, Alfonso Pating, breaks down how homeowner’s insurance works and why climate change is making it unaffordable.

More reports and resources on this topic here.

#179542. RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (957 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

RMI’s Hydrogen Research Is Getting Better. Its Investment Advice Still Falls Short.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies.
  • In a recent development, I have been challenging this tension since January 2024.
  • In a recent development, consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that RMI has become much more realistic about hydrogen demand and competing technologies. That makes the gaps between its findings and its recommendations harder to excuse. Its latest work acknowledges that battery trucks generally have better economics than hydrogen fuel-cell trucks, that Europe needs far less hydrogen in 2030 than it originally targeted, and that low-emissions ammonia still costs substantially more than conventional ammonia. Several recommendations still seek public money to develop the very hydrogen markets the research has found difficult to justify.

In a recent development, I have been challenging this tension since January 2024. RMI matters because governments, investors and industrial companies use its research when deciding where to spend money. Its hydrogen program has made genuine analytical corrections. It has not made all of the accompanying strategic decisions.

In a recent development, consider RMI’s February 2026 report on hydrogen trucking in India. The baseline comparisons find that fuel-cell trucks do not reach battery-electric truck ownership-cost parity through 2040, including the long-haul use case. The report also explores a much more favourable hydrogen price in an alternative sensitivity, which brings fuel-cell trucks closer to parity. Those are different findings, and the baseline matters to investment decisions today.

The report nevertheless recommends hydrogen vehicle subsidies, support for refuelling stations, production incentives and tax relief. It treats a parallel hydrogen-truck market as something to build. The case for spending public money on that market should start with evidence that a particular freight service cannot be served as well or better by batteries. The reported cost advantage of batteries does not disappear when the policy section begins.

The problem reaches beyond India. RMI’s 2025 US hydrogen report says battery trucks have greater market readiness and lower total cost of ownership, especially in the near term, yet calls for hydrogen distribution and refuelling infrastructure along freight corridors. The independent NACFE Run on Less ownership-cost work, developed within RMI’s freight research ecosystem, projects batteries becoming the lowest-cost option across its modelled duty cycles by 2035 without incentives. Hydrogen remains the most expensive option across nearly all of them. These findings support battery infrastructure as the default and a high evidentiary bar for hydrogen exceptions.

RMI already knows how to make appropriate distinctions elsewhere. Its 2026 steel research separates hydrogen used to reduce iron ore from hydrogen burned merely to supply process heat. In the illustrative plant, electric heat requires about 850 GWh a year, compared with 1,300 GWh of electricity to produce enough additional hydrogen for heating. That is the kind of direct service comparison that ought to govern recommendations throughout the organization.

Its new Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance also has a coherent industrial purpose. Fertiliser production already requires ammonia, commonly made with fossil-derived hydrogen. Purchasing lower-emissions ammonia to replace that supply addresses an existing industrial input. It does not require inventing a new energy market for ammonia combustion.

Sources indicate that europe reveals how improved diagnosis can coexist with excessive policy ambition. RMI’s March 2025 recalibration reduced expected mandate-driven renewable hydrogen demand in 2030 to 2.2–2.8 million tons, far below the EU’s original 20-million-ton supply-and-import ambition. Its analysis identifies €13.9 billion in public support under existing mandates, plus €31.7 billion for an accelerated scenario. The combined €45.6 billion deserves a comparison with the other ways industry could obtain the same low-carbon products and services, including direct electrification and imported green materials.

In a recent development, that comparison changes the question for ammonia, steel and refining. A European fertiliser or chemical manufacturer needs ammonia, not necessarily hydrogen manufactured inside Europe. A steelmaker needs iron meeting its grade and emissions requirements. A mill needs process heat at specified temperatures. Governments can pay a premium to preserve domestic capacity for security or resilience, but the benefit must be valued and the public cost made explicit.

Recent findings suggest that my November 2026 European hydrogen assessment applies that approach. In its central 2050 scenario, ammonia produced in Europe with on-site green hydrogen costs approximately €1,222 per ton. Qualifying imported green ammonia costs €745–755 per ton under the model’s assumptions. These are modelled values, not supplier bids. They demonstrate why an analysis that starts with hydrogen production targets can produce the wrong infrastructure plan.

Recent findings suggest that RMI’s 2026 China green ammonia and methanol report acknowledges that green production costs remain two to three times conventional costs and that demand development lags supply ambitions. The report nevertheless discusses expanding ammonia and methanol as energy carriers, including ammonia for electricity. The relevant comparison for electricity is renewable generation with storage and other flexibility, not fossil-derived ammonia alone. RMI has not demonstrated that adding an ammonia combustion pathway wins that comparison.

This is a strategy problem as much as a modelling problem. Using Richard Rumelt’s framework, RMI’s diagnosis has improved, its guiding policy remains too committed to expanding hydrogen markets, and some coherent actions are missing. An economically unfavourable comparison should be able to end an infrastructure recommendation. Instead, it too often generates proposals for subsidies that would make the hydrogen route easier to sell.

Industry observers note that RMI has the expertise to correct this. Its hydrogen recommendations should carry explicit alternative-technology comparisons, investment thresholds and exit criteria. Cross-program review should include the researchers measuring battery costs, industrial electrification, freight operations and grid flexibility. Where hydrogen is an essential chemical input or demonstrably the best means of delivering a service, support it. Where competing technologies win on cost and deployment readiness, stop trying to create demand through policy.

Industry observers note that the full TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines RMI’s US, India, Europe and China reports side by side, including the differences between its findings and recommendations. It also links the original sources and the 2024 critique.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solar module manufacturer Thornova Solar and Nextpower, a provider of advanced solar tracker and structural solutions, marked a milestone in their growing strategic cooperation with the signing of a Master Supply Agreement (MSA).

It has been revealed that the agreement, announced at RE+ 2026, further strengthens the collaboration between the two companies, combining Thornova Solar’s U.S.-made solar modules with Nextpower’s U.S.-manufactured steel frame technology. The expanded effort is designed to deliver increased domestic content opportunities and enhanced structural performance, providing greater value to customers developing utility-scale and commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects across the United States.

According to the companies, integrating advanced steel frame solutions into selected Thornova Solar module series addresses two increasingly notable priorities in the U.S. solar market: maximizing domestic content and improving module resilience under demanding environmental conditions.

The combined solution offers several key benefits:.

The solution is particularly relevant for projects in demanding U.S. environments, including high-wind regions across the Midwest and Southeast, where structural reliability and long-term module performance are critical considerations.

Sources indicate that “The signing of this Master Supply Agreement represents an crucial step in strengthening our relationship with Nextpower and expanding the value we deliver to U.S. customers,” stated Andrea Bodenhagen, global marketing director of Thornova Solar. “By bringing together U.S.-made solar modules and domestically manufactured steel frame technology, we are helping our customers increase domestic content while benefiting from stronger, more resilient module solutions. This is exactly the kind of collaboration needed to advance a competitive U.S. solar manufacturing ecosystem.”.

In a recent development, “We’re excited to deepen our strategic collaboration with Thornova and bring modules featuring Nextpower’s domestically manufactured steel frames to the U.S. market,” said Jenya Meydbray, vice president and general manager of Nextpower. “NX CoreFrame offers a significant opportunity to advance module strength and reliability, addressing industry challenges such as glass breakage and demanding environmental loads while delivering greater confidence to solar developers and owners.”.

The MSA reflects the shared commitment of both companies to strengthening domestic manufacturing and delivering solutions that respond to the evolving technical and commercial requirements of the U.S. solar market.

News item from Thornova Solar and Nextpower.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that some people don't need to fire up "Grand Theft Auto 6" on a gaming console to experience the terror of a chaotic populace. The universe Rockstar Games crafted over two decades is over-the-top, but it has always been a satirical reflection of American society. This reflection also includes how swiftly some of our fellow drivers are willing to resort to violence over the smallest grievance. However, our country's healthcare system hasn't discovered respawning despite how much money we've poured into it.

We asked our readers last week which road rage moments from their real lives most mirrored what they would see in "Grand Theft Auto 6." The responses in the comment section didn't disappoint with how bizarre, hilarious and terrifying these incidents were. Beyond the traditional roadside fistfights, we had a snowball toted like a handgun, altercations with actual firearms and BMW drivers reinforcing their terrible reputation. Without further ado, here are the incidents that wouldn't look out of place in Vice City:.

According to recent reports, back in HS, A friend of mine and I were driving around late night and while stopped at an intersection a guy in a Jeep took the corner really fast and almost sideswiped us. My friend gave him the middle finger out of the sunroof. Next thing we knew, we're in a high-speed chase involving the guy, who tried ramming us off the road multiple times. He caught us in a parking lot, blocked us from leaving and pointed a LARGE revolver at us. I grabbed my buddy's cell phone, held it up and screamed "I'm on the phone with the cops!" (even though I wasn't). That gave us enough time to drive over a curb, ripping his mufflers off, and drive up an embankment and high-tail it to the police station.

Moral of the story: Don't flip people off. Let it go and go on with your day.

Sources indicate that A couple of years ago, I was walking through San Francisco's Embarcadero District on my way to Radwood NorCal (which was held on one of the piers that year). I overheard some yelling and turned my head to see a blue Jeep Cherokee XJ pulled over on the side of the road. The Jeep driver and a random homeless guy were in each other's face, yelling at each other. From what I made out, the driver accused the homeless guy of jaywalking right in front of him and spitting at his Jeep while the homeless guy argued that he was a pedestrian and that he had the right of way. Fortunately, it was just words being exchanged and no physical blows. The Jeep driver decided he had enough and took off with a loud squeal of tires.

It's so long ago that I don't remember what precipitated it, what happened, or how I behaved but here's what I do remember:.

It was late afternoon. I was driving down 580 South through Berkeley, CA on my way to the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge. And here's how it ended: the other driver was on my left, his passenger-side window was open, and suddenly there was a VERY LOUD BANG from something hitting the side of my car. I hit the brakes so he'd shoot past me. He sped off, I kept my distance.

In a recent development, later, I found a strange dent by the rear pillar (1997? Mazda Navajo LX (aka Ford Explorer Sport), like a thumb had pressed in the metal, but no hole in the metal or even the slightest break in the paint.

It has been revealed that I don't know, maybe he fired a .22 at me? A BB gun? Regardless, it was pretty frightening.

In a recent development, I was walking in downtown Chicago. A guy pulls to a stop at a red light at an intersection. He gets out of his car, nonchalantly walks up to a woman standing on the sidewalk waiting to cross the street, slaps her, then immediately walks calmly back to his car just as the light turns green, and drives away*. I assume they knew each other, because the woman did not react even a little, and continued just standing there with zero expression on her face.

*: He got instant karma, as there was a police cruiser 2 cars behind him, who then pulled him over on the next block.

About 15 years ago, my wife and I were sitting in her Chevy Cobalt in a parking spot in front of Hobby Lobby in Lincoln, NE during the holiday shopping season. It was snowing heavily (which will become vital in a moment). We were on the phone with our cable organization trying to figure out a billing error when another car pulls in next to us. The driver opens her door so hard it slams into our passenger door. I roll down the window and say something to the effect of, "Thanks for the door ding." Nothing demeaning. No name-calling. No F-you. Literally just sarcastically stated what I said. Suddenly the husband comes flying around the car screaming at me, tries to open my door (which I quickly locked), and when he realizes he can't get in goes to the front of the car and begins making a snowball out of the fresh snow. He literally holds his arm as if he is going to throw it at me while his wife joins in with the yelling. The cable company rep on our speakerphone is asking us if we need to hang up to call 911. We are in our car dying of laughter at this fool who is going to use a snowball as a weapon.

It has been revealed that as they settle down and start walking into the store, we end our phone conversation and decide to exit our vehicle, as their loud yelling drew a small crowd, so we knew we would be safe. As I open my door, the husband and wife come flying back out of the store yelling at us for door-dinging THEIR car (I hadn't) and the husband slips in the snow and eats it. Serves him right.

Industry observers note that was first in line waiting to turn left on a red light that had an advance green. I heard sirens, so when the light changed to green I stayed still.

The 5 Series BMW behind me was blaring his horn and making a verbal commotion. Then he decided to swing around me on the right side to make the left-hand turn.

According to recent reports, he was so busy looking at me sitting there that he almost didn't notice the ambulance right in front of him. (with lights and sirens). He slammed his brakes to a very sudden stop and the ambulance had to swerve around him.

According to recent reports, I saw him look in the rearview mirror at me. I smiled and waved.

Recent findings suggest that this is more GTA San Andreas. I worked as a buyer in California for a large dealer that had blue uniform shirts (hint hint). My coworker was test-driving a customer car we were making an offer on, which was a bright blue Dodge Challenger with aftermarket matching blue rims.

He's sitting at a stoplight in his blue work shirt and bright blue car when a guy dressed completely in red, who was walking down the street, started yelling and running towards him. Luckily, the light turned green and my coworker gunned it before the guy got too close and things escalated further.

In a recent development, this was in the '90s. I was taking the Super Shuttle back to BWI from downtown DC and on the side of the road, a Mercedes and a BMW were pulled over and two dudes in suits were duking it out. Full-on fisticuffs in the breakdown lane, black eyes and bloody ties!

Stopped at a red light that had been red for about five seconds before I got to it. Dude in a black BMW 5 Series rolled up behind me and started blaring his horn. When that had no effect, he got out screaming with rage and started to approach my driver's door.

At which time, seeing no cross-traffic, I accelerated through the red and called 911. He got back in his car, raced through the red after me. Being about six blocks from the police station, I told the operator not to bother sending the police: I'd bring him to them.

He followed me right to the police station, tailgating me and blaring his horn the whole way as screaming out the window and giving me the middle finger. And boy was he in for a nasty surprise when we got there.

I love some cartoon violence. When I lived in Vancouver, a number of years ago, I'd just hopped off the bus downtown. A dude ran past me, reached out and snatched the purse off the shoulder of an older lady. He took off faster than I expected him to be able to run. If he'd just kept going, he'd have been home free. Instead, he looked over his shoulder to see if anyone was chasing him (three of us were)... and ran full speed into a glass bus shelter. Glass exploded everywhere, he hit the ground like wet cement and started bleeding from a decent head wound, and it was fantastic. Cartoon violence, instant karma, and a grateful lady who bought the three of us Starbucks for giving chase.

Stellantis CEO More Bullish on EVs than Stellantis CEOs of Old, But Sings Same Boring Song

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stellantis has never been a bastion of EV enthusiasm and progress.
  • According to recent reports, stellantis is still dragging its feet on EVs in the United States and elsewhere, but the assumption at the top seems to have shifted to believing that the whole industry will transition over the EVs eventually.
  • CEO Antonio Filosa recently noted that the US would eventually embrace electric vehicles, but that EV adoption is just slower here than in other regions (where there’s a combination of much more model choice, more government support, more EV awareness, and not so many barriers at the dealer level).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stellantis has never been a bastion of EV enthusiasm and progress. Back in the day (about 10 years ago), Sergio Marchionne was a very openly, blatantly anti-EV CEO. He actually asked customers to not buy their first electric car, the Fiat 500e.

According to recent reports, stellantis is still dragging its feet on EVs in the United States and elsewhere, but the assumption at the top seems to have shifted to believing that the whole industry will transition over the EVs eventually. Just not today.

CEO Antonio Filosa recently noted that the US would eventually embrace electric vehicles, but that EV adoption is just slower here than in other regions (where there’s a combination of much more model choice, more government support, more EV awareness, and not so many barriers at the dealer level).

Filosa notes that the share of new auto sales that are electrics is just 7% this year, about the same as five years ago. “It has been a bubble driven by regulation. ​But then, when the administration has decided to deregulate, the ⁠consumers have been preferring other powertrains,” he added. It’s hard to argue with such claims. There are barriers to more sales, as already noted, but Americans apparently haven’t stormed dealerships looking for EVs except in certain rare circumstances. The fact is: more vehicle options and probably better consumer awareness have led to countries across Asia, Europe, and South America rapidly increasing their EV adoption rates and catching up to or passing the US market.

“The level of magnitude and the speed of ​transition is going to be lower for sure than other regions,” Filosa predicted, but he said he “truly” believed the market would eventually boom in the US.

Industry observers note that as others have noted in recent times, Filosa states the automobile market is becoming more regional again, less global. That may be the case, but it is also clear that some EV companies, most notably BYD, are rapidly expanding across the globe and helping to spur on much quicker EV adoption. The concern with the US is that it’s blocking such companies with severe 100% (and higher) tariffs. So, the US is getting no boost from these highly competitive new vehicles.

What we have seen — whether in Europe, China, Australia, or Ecuador — is that markets that have a lot of EV choice and that have automakers trying to sell a lot of EVs can, in fact, find buyers. So, it’s hard to believe the claim that consumers in the US just don’t want EVs. It seems more likely to me that we don’t have enough EV options, automakers don’t try very hard to sell their EVs if they don’t have to, and there are significant barriers to put in front of consumers when they go to car dealerships. Is Filosa right — that Americans just don’t want EVs that much yet without serious incentives from the government? Or is he just singing the same old disingenuous or wrong song in saying that Americans by and large aren’t ready for EVs yet?

LDV eDeliver 5 — A Chinese Bargain?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A bargain electric van from China — the LDV eDeliver 5.
  • On the same day that we looked at the Kia PV5, we were also able to check out the LDV eDeliver 5.
  • Recent findings suggest that the second dealership also sold Geely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A bargain electric van from China — the LDV eDeliver 5. “The tide is changing; people are more on board with Chinese cars and electric vehicles” in Australia. And it has 50% more cargo space than the Korean competition (6.6 cubic metres). For the same price!

On the same day that we looked at the Kia PV5, we were also able to check out the LDV eDeliver 5. Chatting to the sales rep (Daniel), we discovered they had sold and delivered the one they had on the lot. Nevertheless, he told us some great stories and we caught up with the van at another dealership down the road later in the week.

Recent findings suggest that the second dealership also sold Geely. The lot was full of them, and the rep told us several times how fast the Geely EX2 and EX5 were selling. Thank you, President Trump, and Supreme Leader Khamenei. Sales of Geely in Australia have doubled since the war started!

Anyway, back to the LDV eDeliver 5. For the curious, LDV stands for Leyland DAF Vans. After the collapse of British Leyland, the brand was sold to SAIC (along with MG). Since the eDeliver 5 launch in July, 77 units have sold in Australia. I felt that the number should be higher, agreeing with the comment found under the PV5 article: “High mileage work vehicles are the first frontier for EVs, not the last. That’s where there is the most financial benefit.” Sadly, though, commercial vans which work so hard around the suburbs, especially near Christmas, have been the slowest segment to electrify in Australia.

Another commentator made the valid point: “Business and fleet vehicles have consistent, predictable daily mileage, high daily mileage, thus huge annual battery utilization (therefore huge fuel savings), they don’t burn a ton of expensive fuel, and are purchased by financially rational decision makers.”.

Recent findings suggest that so, why aren’t more electric vans being bought in Australia? Running costs are lower, they are more comfortable, and the sticker price is now below price parity. Daniel and I had a fruitful discussion and came to the conclusion that the main thing stopping electric vans from being taken up in large numbers by fleet operators was the matter of the “fuel card.” It is complicated on the road because of multiple apps and providers, and even more if the van driver charges at home. How do we reimburse for home charging?

It has been revealed that surely this hurdle is not that hard to surmount — especially for contractors and owner operators. We’ll see as fuel insecurity in Australia continues. One owner reported back to Daniel that he has spent AU$3,000 to charge his eDeliver 5 over the past 50,000 km, compared with a diesel fuel bill of AU$14,000 for his old diesel van over the same distance. “Even if I sold the LDV van for nothing after 5 years, I would still be ahead.”.

According to recent reports, apparently, some couriers are doing 500 km a day around the Brisbane suburbs. With a range of 320 km from its LFP batteries, the eDeliver 5 would have to top up during the day. Near our home in the northern suburbs of Brisbane, some service stations have installed high-speed chargers (BP Pulse is one example). I very rarely see anyone charging there. Perhaps that’s the charging that will be used by electric delivery vans. LDV also makes larger models, the eDeliver 7 and 9.

Daniel usually only sells two vans a year. He tells me that he has sold five eDeliver 5’s in the past 6 weeks! August to November is their peak time for sales. The tide is indeed changing. The diesel Deliver 5 is AU$10,000–12,000 cheaper than the electric, but with the large kilometres they drive it would not be long before this difference was covered by fuel savings. The eDeliver has V2L capability, putting out 6.6 kWh charge for added convenience. One local customer runs a fridge in the back of the van from the V2L capability.

As an example of the effect of the Iran/USA war, Daniel told us of a customer who bought a fresh diesel ute 3 weeks before the war started and then came back and wanted to trade it in. He even offered his wife’s car as part of the deal. But the numbers just wouldn’t add up.

Service costs roughly $735 every two years or 30,000 km on the eDeliver 5. Compare this with the Toyota HiAce. The diesel needs a service every 10,000 km. Daniel tells me that during EV service, they check the oil in the gearbox and the coolant for the battery. “Couriers like the power on/off button. A lot of people are screen scared.” The eDeliver 5 has a fob, it is a cheaper option than connectivity.

In a recent development, of course, a Facebook page has been started. I joined it seeking more real-life experiences.

“I have one that I’ve been driving for a month now. I use it for work and have tools in the back, so the weight of the car is 2.4 tonnes. With driving around town (mostly city and some highway). I get around 250 km before I have to charge again from about 10%.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a great ride and very comfy. I do maybe 100 km per day, so charge every second or third. Works great for me.”.

Industry observers note that “There has been a seismic shift in consumer behaviour due to recent geo-political tensions, fuel insecurity, and surging diesel costs,” said Dinesh Chinnappa, the general manager of LDV Australia. “With that in mind we brought forward our plans to introduce the LDV eDeliver 5 to the Australian market, which is why stock will initially be limited.”.

Sources indicate that you can check out the specs here. Of course it has all the safety features you would expect. For those who like to watch, check out the video review of the eDeliver 7.

There are several small cargo vans now available on the Australian market. I will endeavour to check out a few more and report back to CleanTechnica readers. As we hurtle towards Christmas and the online orders increase, I expect to see many more electric Santas delivering parcels to front doors in the suburbs of Brisbane.
